nodes.name: HS-derivation (one-dimensional)
nodes.statement: A sequence $(D_i:R\to R)_{i\in {\mathds{N}}}$ is an HS-derivation (over $k$) if and only if the corresponding map $$\mathbb{D}:R\to R\llbracket X\rrbracket,\ \ \ \mathbb{D}(r)=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}D_i(r)X^i$$ is a ring ($k$-algebra) homomorphism and a section of the projection map $R\llbracket X\rrbracket\to R$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Formal group actions and model theory
nodes.statement_short: A sequence of maps D_i is an HS-derivation iff the induced map R -> R[[X]] is a ring homomorphism that is a section of the projection.

nodes.name: Iterative HS-derivation
nodes.statement: The standard iterativity condition may be expressed using the following diagram \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{R \ar[rr]^{\mathbb{D}} \ar[d]_{\mathbb{D}} & & R\llbracket X\rrbracket \ar[d]^{\mathbb{D}\llbracket X\rrbracket} \\ R\llbracket X\rrbracket\ar[rr]^{X\mapsto X+Y} & & R\llbracket X,Y\rrbracket,} \end{equation*} i.e. $\mathbb{D}$ is iterative if and only if the diagram above is commutative.
nodes.section: 1.1 Formal group actions and model theory
nodes.statement_short: An HS-derivation is iterative iff the diagram expressing compatibility with X -> X+Y commutes.

nodes.name: Truncated iterative HS-derivations as finite group scheme actions
nodes.statement: We start from the truncated iterativity diagram, which is just a truncation of the diagram above expressing the standard iterativity of HS-derivations \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{R \ar[rr]^{\mathbb{D}} \ar[d]_{\mathbb{D}} & & R[v_m] \ar[d]^{\mathbb{D}[v_m]} \\ R[w_m]\ar[rr]^{c_R} & & R[w_m,v_m].} \end{equation*} Here $c_R(w_m)=v_m+w_m$ gives a Hopf algebra structure over $R$. Using the tensor product over the base field $k$, we obtain the following diagram. \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{R \ar[rr]^{\mathbb{D}\ \ \ \ } \ar[d]_{\mathbb{D}} & & k[v_m]\otimes R \ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}_{k[v_m]}\otimes \mathbb{D}} \\ k[v_m]\otimes R\ar[rr]^{c\otimes \mathrm{id}_R\ \ \ \ } & & k[v_m]\otimes k[v_m]\otimes R} \end{equation*} Going to the opposite category (of $k$-schemes), we see that we get exactly the diagram expressing the mixed associativity of a group scheme action \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{R & & \ar[ll]_{\widetilde{\mathbb{D}}} \mathfrak{g}\times X \\ \mathfrak{g}\times X \ar[u]^{\widetilde{\mathbb{D}}} & & \ar[ll]_{\mu \times \mathrm{id}_X} \ar[u]_{\mathrm{id}_{\mathfrak{g}}\times \widetilde{\mathbb{D}}} \mathfrak{g}\times \mathfrak{g}\times X,} \end{equation*} where $X=\mathrm{Spec}(R)$ and $\mathfrak{g}=\ker(\mathrm{Fr}^m_{\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}})$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Formal group actions and model theory
nodes.statement_short: After tensoring and passing to the opposite category, the truncated iterativity diagram becomes the mixed-associativity diagram of an action of ker(Fr^m) on Spec(R).

nodes.name: Standing assumption on the base field k
nodes.statement: In the entire paper, $k$ will be a perfect field of characteristic $p>0$ (unless we clearly say that $\mathrm{char}(k)=0$).
nodes.statement_short: k is a perfect field of characteristic p>0 throughout.

nodes.name: Affine group scheme
nodes.statement: The category of \emph{affine group schemes} over $k$ is the category opposite to the category of \emph{Hopf algebras} over $k$ \cite[Section 1.4]{Water} (or it is the category of representable functors from $k$-algebras to groups, see \cite[Section 1.2]{Water}).

nodes.name: Truncated group scheme
nodes.statement: A \emph{truncated group scheme} \cite{Chase2} over $k$ is an affine group scheme whose universe is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Spec}(k[X_1,\ldots,X_e]/(X_1^{p^m},\ldots,X_e^{p^m}))$.

nodes.name: No truncated group schemes in characteristic zero (Cartier)
nodes.statement: If $\mathrm{char}(k)=0$, then by a theorem of Cartier \cite[Section 11.4]{Water} all Hopf algebras over $k$ are reduced, so there are no truncated group schemes.
nodes.label: notrunzero

nodes.name: Formal group
nodes.statement: The category of \emph{formal groups} over $k$ is the category opposite to the category of \emph{complete Hopf algebras} over $k$ (or the category of representable functors from complete $k$-algebras to groups, see \cite[Chapter VII]{Hazew}).

nodes.name: e-dimensional formal group law
nodes.statement: There is a correspondence between smooth formal groups (the underlying complete algebra is the power series algebra in $e$ variables) and formal group laws, where an $e$-dimensional formal group law over $k$, is a power series in $2e$ variables formally satisfying the group axioms, see \cite[Sect. 9.1]{Hazew}.
nodes.statement_short: Smooth formal groups correspond to formal group laws: power series in 2e variables formally satisfying the group axioms.

nodes.name: Truncated group schemes are formal groups
nodes.statement: Note that a truncated group scheme is both an affine group scheme and a formal group.
conclusions: a truncated group scheme is both an affine group scheme and a formal group

nodes.name: Tuple of variables X
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{X}$ denote the tuple of variables $(X_1,\ldots,X_e)$.

nodes.name: Multi-index monomial X^n
nodes.statement: For a tuple $\mathbf{n}=(n_1,\ldots,n_e)$ of natural numbers, we denote $X_1^{n_1}\ldots X_e^{n_e}$ by $\mathbf{X}^{\mathbf{n}}$.

nodes.name: Truncated polynomial ring k[v_m]
nodes.statement: Let $k[\mathbf{v}_m]$ denote the ring $k[\mathbf{X}]/(X_1^{p^m},\ldots,X_e^{p^m})$.

nodes.name: Index set [l]
nodes.statement: For a positive integer $l$, let $[l]$ denote the set $\{0,\ldots,l-1\}$.

nodes.name: Truncated group scheme g
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a group scheme over $k$ whose underlying scheme is $\mathrm{Spec}(k[\mathbf{v}_m])$.

nodes.name: Algebraic group G
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be an algebraic group over $k$.

nodes.name: Formal group law F
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be an $e$-dimensional formal group law over $k$.

nodes.name: Augmentation ideal
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{G}$ be an affine group scheme over $k$, $H$ the corresponding Hopf algebra and $\mathfrak{m}$ be the kernel of the counit map $H\to k$ (the \emph{augmentation ideal}).
nodes.statement_short: For an affine group scheme with Hopf algebra H, the augmentation ideal is the kernel of the counit H -> k.

nodes.name: Frobenius twist and Frobenius morphism
nodes.statement: Using the base-change given by the automorphism $\mathrm{Fr}^m:k\to k$ we get the affine group scheme $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Fr}^m}$ over $k$ and a group scheme morphism $\mathrm{Fr}^m_{\mathfrak{G}}:\mathfrak{G}\to \mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Fr}^m}$.
nodes.statement_short: Base change along Fr^m gives the twisted group scheme G^{Fr^m} and the Frobenius morphism Fr^m_G.

nodes.name: m-th Frobenius kernel G[m]
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{G}[m]$ be the kernel of $\mathrm{Fr}^m_{\mathfrak{G}}$ which is a truncated $k$-group scheme. (In the case of a commutative group scheme $A$, $A[m]$ often denotes the kernel of multiplication by $m$ and ``our'' $A[m]$ is often denoted by $A[\mathrm{Fr}^m]$. Since we do not consider the kernel of multiplication by $m$ in this paper, we prefer our simplified notation.)
nodes.statement_short: G[m] denotes the kernel of the m-th Frobenius morphism, a truncated group scheme.

nodes.name: Quotient Hopf algebra H[m]
nodes.statement: It corresponds to the quotient Hopf algebra $$H[m]:=H/\mathrm{Fr}^m(\mathfrak{m})H.$$

nodes.name: Formalization as limit of Frobenius kernels (Manin)
nodes.statement: We get a direct system of truncated $k$-group schemes $(\mathfrak{G}[n])_{n\in {\mathds{N}}}$. If $\mathfrak{G}=G$, then $\underrightarrow{\lim}(G[n])$ coincides with $\widehat{G}$, the formal group which is the formalization of $G$ (see \cite[Lemma 1.1]{Manin}).
conclusions: $\underrightarrow{\lim}(G[n])$ coincides with $\widehat{G}$, the formal group which is the formalization of $G$
nodes.statement_short: The Frobenius kernels G[n] form a direct system whose limit is the formalization of G.

nodes.name: Formal group as limit of its truncations (Manin)
nodes.statement: Similarly, for a complete Hopf algebra $\mathcal{H}$, we have the analogous quotient $\mathcal{H}[m]$ which is a Hopf algebra and also a complete Hopf algebra. Hence for a formal group $F$, we have a direct system of truncated group schemes $F[m]$ and in this case we get that $F=\underrightarrow{\lim} F[m]$, see \cite[Lemma 1.1]{Manin} again.
conclusions: $F=\underrightarrow{\lim} F[m]$
nodes.statement_short: A formal group F is the direct limit of its truncated group schemes F[m].

nodes.name: Integrability of truncated group schemes
nodes.statement: One may ask whether any truncated group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ can be integrated i.e. whether there is a formal group law $F$ such that $F[m]=\mathfrak{g}$. For $e=1$, the answer is positive if and only if $\mathfrak{g}$ is commutative \cite[Corollary 5.7.4]{Hazew} (see \cite[Example 5.7.8]{Hazew} for an example of a non-commutative $\mathfrak{g}$).
nodes.statement_short: For e=1 a truncated group scheme comes from a formal group law iff it is commutative.
nodes.label: intgs

nodes.name: Frobenius filtration of g
nodes.statement: For the truncated group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$, we get a finite direct system of truncated group schemes $$0=\mathfrak{g}[0]<\mathfrak{g}[1]<\ldots <\mathfrak{g}[m-1]<\mathfrak{g}[m]=\mathfrak{g}.$$ The group schemes in this direct system may be described as follows. Let $i\in [m+1]$ and $\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{Fr}^i}$ be the group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ twisted by the $i$-th power of the Frobenius map. Then we have a group scheme morphism $\mathrm{Fr}_{\mathfrak{g}}^i:\mathfrak{g}\to \mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{Fr}^i}$ such that $$\ker(\mathrm{Fr}_{\mathfrak{g}}^i)=\mathfrak{g}[i],\ \ \ \mathrm{Fr}_{\mathfrak{g}}^i(\mathfrak{g})=\mathfrak{g}^{\mathrm{Fr}^i}[m-i].$$
nodes.statement_short: g has a finite chain of Frobenius kernels g[i], with ker(Fr^i)=g[i] and image g^{Fr^i}[m-i].
nodes.label: gm

nodes.name: Multi-dimensional (truncated) HS-derivation
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item An \emph{$e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$} is a $k$-algebra homomorphism $$\mathbb{D}:R\to R\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket$$ which is a section of the projection map $$R\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket\to R,\ \ \ H\mapsto H(\mathbf{0}).$$ \item An \emph{$m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$} is a $k$-algebra homomorphism $$\mathbb{D}:R\to R[\mathbf{v}_m]$$ which is a section of the projection map $R[\mathbf{v}_m]\to R$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: An (m-truncated) e-dimensional HS-derivation is a k-algebra section R -> R[[X]] (resp. R[v_m]) of the projection.
nodes.label: hstrdef

nodes.name: Basic facts on e-dimensional HS-derivations
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item From any $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$ over $k$ and any positive integer $n$, we get in an obvious way (i.e. by post-composing with the quotient map $R\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket\to R[\mathbf{v}_n]$) an $n$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ which we denote by $\mathbb{D}[n]$. \item Let us denote $\mathbb{D}(r)$ by $\sum_{\mathbf{i}} D_{\mathbf{i}}(r)\mathbf{X}^{\mathbf{i}}$. Using such a notation, an $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$ is a sequence $$\mathbb{D}=(D_{\mathbf{i}}:R\to R)_{\mathbf{i}\in {\mathds{N}}^e}$$ satisfying the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item $D_{\mathbf{0}}=\mathrm{id}_R$, \item each $D_{\mathbf{i}}$ is $k$-linear, \item for any $x,y\in R$ we have $$D_{\mathbf{i}}(xy)=\sum_{\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}}D_{\mathbf{j}}(x)D_{\mathbf{k}}(y).$$ \end{itemize} \item Each $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$ gives the following tuple of (1-dimensional) HS-derivations on $R$: $$\mathbb{D}_1:=(D_{(i,0,\ldots,0)})_{i\in {\mathds{N}}},\ \ldots \ ,\mathbb{D}_e:=(D_{(0,\ldots,0,i)})_{i\in {\mathds{N}}}.$$ On the level of $k$-algebra maps, the above $m$-truncated HS-derivations correspond to the composition of $\mathbb{D}:R\to R\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket$ with the appropriate projection map $R\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket\to R\llbracket X\rrbracket$. \item On the other hand, each $e$-tuple of (1-dimensional) HS-derivations on $R$ gives an $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$, e.g. for $e=2$ and $\mathbb{D}_1,\mathbb{D}_2:R\to R\llbracket X\rrbracket$ we get the $2$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ given by the composition below \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{2.5pc}\xymatrixrowsep{1.5pc}\xymatrix{R \ar[r]^{\mathbb{D}_1\ \ \ } & R\llbracket X\rrbracket \ar[r]^{\mathbb{D}_2\llbracket X\rrbracket\ \ \ \ } & R\llbracket X,Y\rrbracket .} \end{equation*} \noindent However, not all $e$-dimensional HS-derivations on $R$ can be obtained in such a way. In fact an $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ is not necessarily determined by the $e$-tuple $\mathbb{D}_1,\ldots,\mathbb{D}_e$ from $(3)$. For example consider the (truncated) case when $p=2$ and $m=1$. If $\partial$ is a non-zero derivation on $R$, then the map $$\mathbb{D}(r)=r+\partial(r)(X+(X^2))(Y+(Y^2))$$ is a non-zero $1$-truncated $2$-dimensional HS-derivation, but the corresponding $1$-truncated $1$-dimensional HS-derivations from $(3)$ are the zero maps. \item All the above (for $n\leqslant m$) applies to $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations (after replacing ``${\mathds{N}}$'' with ``$[p^m]$'' and ``$\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket$'' with ``$[\mathbf{v}_m]$''). \item We can extend Definition \ref{hstrdef} to define $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations from $R$ to $S$ (we do not require anything about the sections here). \item Our $m$-truncated $1$-dimensional HS-derivations correspond to the \emph{higher derivations of length $p^m-1$} from \cite{mat}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Truncations D[n], coordinate description via operators D_i, the associated 1-dimensional HS-derivations, and an example showing these need not determine D.
nodes.label: edimrem

nodes.name: Etale lifting with nilpotent kernels
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that the condition ``$N^2=0$'' from \cite[p. 193]{mat} may be replaced with the condition ``$N$ is nilpotent'' (see e.g. Remark on page 199 of \cite{mat0}).
nodes.statement_short: In the definition of an étale map the square-zero condition can be replaced by nilpotency.

nodes.name: Unique extension of HS-derivations along étale maps
nodes.statement: Assume that $R\to S$ is an \'{e}tale $k$-algebra map. Then any ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$ uniquely extends to an ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $S$.
conclusions: any ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$ uniquely extends to an ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}'$ on $S$
nodes.label: etalehs

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: The proof goes almost exactly as in \cite[theorem 27.2]{mat}, so we will just sketch the main inductive step which makes clear how the \'{e}tale assumption is used. We apply the induction on the truncation degree. Assume that for $l\in {\mathds{N}}$ (resp. $l<m$) we have extended $\mathbb{D}[l]$ to an $l$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation $\mathbb{D}':=(D'_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}<[p^l]^e}$ on $S$. Consider the following diagram \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{2.5pc}\xymatrixrowsep{1.5pc}\xymatrix{& S[\mathbf{X}]/(X_1^{p^l},\ldots,X_e^{p^l}) & \\ S \ar[ur]^-{\mathbb{D}'} \ar@{-->}[rr] & & S[\mathbf{X}]/(X_1^{p^{l+1}},\ldots,X_e^{p^{l+1}}) \ar[ul]_{\pi} \\ & R \ar[ul]^{f} \ar[ur]_{\mathbb{D}[l+1]} & } \end{equation*} where $\pi$ is the quotient map. Then $(\ker \pi)^{e+1}=0$, so $\ker(\pi)$ is nilpotent. Since the map $R\to S$ is \'{e}tale, we get a unique $k$-algebra map $$S\to S[\mathbf{X}]/(X_1^{p^{l+1}},\ldots,X_e^{p^{l+1}})$$ completing the diagram above.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: induction on the truncation degree, lifting via the étale property across a nilpotent kernel.

nodes.name: Generalizations of Definition 3.1
nodes.statement: Proposition \ref{etalehs} enables us to generalize Definition \ref{hstrdef} in the following way. \begin{enumerate} \item Since the localization maps are \'{e}tale (see \cite[p. 193]{mat}), any ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ uniquely extends to an ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on a localization of $R$. \item By $(1)$, we get a notion of an ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on any scheme over $k$. \item Proposition \ref{etalehs} generalizes to schemes over $k$. \item The notion of an ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on a scheme $V$ is a special case of the notion of a \emph{$\underline{\mathcal{D}}$-structure} on a scheme $V$, see \cite{MS}. We will discuss possible generalizations of the results of this paper to the context of \cite{MS} in Section \ref{msecop}. \item It is easy to generalize the assumptions of Proposition \ref{etalehs} to include the case of ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivations \emph{from $R$ to $S$}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: By étale extension, HS-derivations extend to localizations and hence to schemes, as special cases of D-structures.
nodes.label: defgen

nodes.name: Ring of constants, strict, absolute constants
nodes.statement: If $\mathbb{D}$ is an ($m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$, then we define the following. \begin{enumerate} \item The \emph{ring of constants} of $(R,\mathbb{D})$ is $$\ker(D_{(1,0,\ldots,0)})\cap \ldots \cap \ker(D_{(0,\ldots,0,1)}).$$ Clearly, $R^p$ is contained in the ring of constants of $(R,\mathbb{D})$. \item We call $(R,\mathbb{D})$ \emph{strict}, if the ring of constants of $\mathbb{D}$ coincides with $R^p$. \item The \emph{ring of absolute constants} of $(R,\mathbb{D})$ is $$\bigcap_{\mathbf{i}\neq \mathbf{0}}\ker(D_{\mathbf{i}}).$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.definiendum: ring of constants; strict; ring of absolute constants
nodes.statement_short: Constants: common kernel of the first-order operators; strict: constants equal R^p; absolute constants: common kernel of all D_i, i nonzero.
nodes.label: firstdefstrict

nodes.name: p^m-th powers are absolute constants
nodes.statement: If $\mathbb{D}$ is an (resp. $m$-truncated) $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$, then $R^{p^{\infty}}$ (resp. $R^{p^m}$) is contained in the ring of absolute constants. It is easy to see (e.g. in the $m$-truncated case) considering $\mathbb{D}:R\to R[\mathbf{v}_m]$ as a ring homomorphism and taking the $p^m$-th power.
nodes.statement_short: R^{p^m} (resp. R^{p^infty}) lies in the ring of absolute constants.

nodes.name: HS-ring
nodes.statement: The couple $(R,\mathbb{D})$ will be usually denoted by $\mathbf{R}$ and called an ($m$-truncated $e$-dimensional) \emph{HS-ring}. Similarly, we get the notions of \emph{HS-fields}, \emph{HS-extension}, etc.

nodes.name: g-derivation
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item A \emph{$\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V$} is a $k$-group scheme action of $\mathfrak{g}$ on $V$ (see Section 12 in \cite{MuAbel}). \item A \emph{$\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $R$} is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $\mathrm{Spec}(R)$. \item We naturally get the notions of a \emph{$\mathfrak{g}$-ring}, a \emph{$\mathfrak{g}$-field} and a \emph{$\mathfrak{g}$-extension}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A g-derivation on V is a group scheme action of g on V; on R it is one on Spec(R).

nodes.name: g-derivations as g-iterative truncated HS-derivations
nodes.statement: A $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $R$ is the same as an $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$ satisfying a ``$\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity'' rule. It is easy to see that the trivial action of the unit morphism corresponds to the condition $D_{\mathbf{0}}=\mathrm{id}_R$ and the diagram expressing the mixed associativity of the $k$-group scheme action $d$ is the following ``$\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity'' diagram \begin{equation*} \xymatrix{R \ar[r]^d \ar[d]_d & R[\mathbf{v}_m] \ar[d]^{d[\mathbf{v}_m]} \\ R[\mathbf{w}_m]\ar[r]^{c} & R[\mathbf{w}_m,\mathbf{v}_m]} \end{equation*} where $\mathbf{w}_m$ is another ``$m$-truncated $e$-tuple of variables'' and $c$ is the Hopf algebra comultiplication given by $\mathfrak{g}$. Therefore for an arbitrary $k$-scheme $V$, any $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V$ is also an $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $V$ over $k$ in the sense of Remark \ref{defgen}(2).
nodes.statement_short: A g-derivation is an m-truncated e-dimensional HS-derivation satisfying the g-iterativity diagram given by the comultiplication.
nodes.label: gderint

nodes.name: g-iterativity via structural constants
nodes.statement: We will give another interpretation of the $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity condition. Suppose that the matrix (in the standard basis) of the $k$-linear comultiplication map $c$ from Remark \ref{gderint} has the form $(c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}})$. Suppose also that $\mathbb{D}=(D_{\mathbf{i}})_{\mathbf{i}}$ is an $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivation on $R$ over $k$. Then $\mathbb{D}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation if and only if for all $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}$ we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}\circ D_{\mathbf{i}}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}D_{\mathbf{k}}.$$
nodes.statement_short: With structural constants c of the comultiplication, D is a g-derivation iff D_j∘D_i = sum_k c^k_{i,j} D_k.
nodes.label: gderint2

nodes.name: g-derivations for products of group schemes
nodes.statement: If $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_1\times \ldots \times \mathfrak{g}_e$ (product of finite group schemes), then we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item For any $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$ and $i\leqslant e$, $\mathbb{D}_i$ from Remark \ref{edimrem} is a $\mathfrak{g}_i$-derivation and we have $$D_{(i_1,\ldots,i_e)}=D_{1,i_1}\circ \ldots \circ D_{e,i_e}.$$ \item If for any any $i\leqslant e$, $\mathbb{D}_i$ is an $\mathfrak{g}_i$-derivation, and we have $D_{i,i'}\circ D_{j,j'}= D_{j,j'}\circ D_{i,i'}$ for all $i,j\leqslant e$ and $i',j'\in {\mathds{N}}$, then the formula $$D_{(i_1,\ldots,i_e)}=D_{1,i_1}\circ \ldots \circ D_{e,i_e}$$ defines a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a product of group schemes, g-derivations correspond to commuting tuples of g_i-derivations via composition.
nodes.label: frometo1

nodes.name: Examples of g-iterativity rules
nodes.statement: We give below several examples of $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity rules. \begin{enumerate} \item A sequence of $e$ commuting iterative $m$-truncated HS-derivations from \cite{K3} is the same as a $\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}^e[m]$-derivation (see Fact \ref{frometo1}). \item Let $G$ be the unipotent algebraic group of dimension $2$ given by the cocycle $$\frac{(X+Y)^p-X^p-Y^p}{p},$$ see \cite[p. 171]{serre1988algebraic}. \\ Assume that $p=2$ and $\mathbb{D}$ is an $m$-truncated $2$-dimensional HS-derivation. Then $\mathbb{D}$ is a $G[m]$-derivation if and only if $$D_{(k,l)}\circ D_{(i,j)}=\sum\limits_{t=0}^{\min(j,l)}\frac{(i+k+t)!}{i!k!t!} \frac{(j+l-2t)!}{(j-t)!(l-t)!}\;\; D_{(i+k+t,j+l-2t)}.$$ In particular, we have the following formulas which actually describe the $G[m]$-iterativity rule fully: $$D_{(0,j)}\circ D_{(i,0)}=D_{(i,j)}=D_{(i,0)}\circ D_{(0,j)},$$ $$D_{(k,0)}\circ D_{(i,0)}={i+k\choose i}D_{(i+k,0)},$$ $$D_{(0,1)}\circ D_{(0,i)}=(i+1)D_{(0,i+1)}+D_{(1,i-1)}.$$ The first author described in \cite{Hoff2} a modification of the theory of separably closed fields with higher derivations from \cite{MeWo} using the iterativity rules coming from algebraic groups similar to the one considered here (groups of Witt vectors). \item Let $G$ be $\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}\rtimes \mathbb{G}_{\rm{m}}$, where the group operation on $\mathbb{G}_{\rm{m}}$ is given by $X+Y+XY$. Hence the group operation on $G$ is given by $$(X_1,Y_1)*(X_2,Y_2)=(X_1+X_2+Y_1X_2,Y_1+Y_2+Y_1Y_2).$$ Let $\mathbb{D}$ be an $m$-truncated $2$-dimensional HS-derivation. Then $\mathbb{D}$ is a $G[m]$-derivation if and only if $$D_{(k,l)}\circ D_{(i,j)} = \sum\limits_{t=0}^{\min(k,j)}\sum\limits_{s=0}^{\min(l,j-t)} \frac{(i+k)!}{i!(k-t)!t!}\;\frac{(j+l-t-s)!}{(j-t-s)!(l-s)!s!}\;\; D_{(i+k,j+l-t-s)}.$$ In particular, we have $$D_{(0,l)}\circ D_{(i,0)}=D_{(i,l)}.$$ But the above formula does not apply for the other choice of coordinates $$D_{(1,0)}\circ D_{(0,1)}=D_{(1,1)}+D_{(1,0)}\neq D_{(1,1)}=D_{(0,1)}\circ D_{(1,0)}.$$ We also have the following ``additive coordinate'' rule $$D_{(1,0)}\circ D_{(i,0)}=(i+1)D_{(1+i,0)}=D_{(i,0)}\circ D_{(1,0)},$$ and the ``multiplicative coordinate'' rule $$D_{(0,1)}\circ D_{(0,i)}=(i+1)D_{(0,i+1)}+iD_{(0,i)}=D_{(0,i)}\circ D_{(0,1)}.$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit G[m]-iterativity rules for G_a^e, a 2-dimensional unipotent group (p=2), and G_a ⋊ G_m.
nodes.label: gitex

nodes.name: e-dimensional F-derivations are determined by 1-dimensional ones
nodes.statement: We see that all the $e$-dimensional HS-derivations in the example above are determined by the 1-dimensional HS-derivations $\mathbb{D}_1,\ldots,\mathbb{D}_e$ from Remark \ref{edimrem}(3). It may be shown (using Lemma \ref{newton} below) that this is the case for an arbitrary $F$-derivation (or a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation).
nodes.label: onedimenough

nodes.name: Structural constants of the comultiplication
nodes.statement: Let $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}$ be as in Remark \ref{gderint2}. For a tuple of natural numbers $\mathbf{n}=(n_1,\ldots,n_e)$, the sum $n_1+\ldots+n_e$ is denoted by $|\mathbf{n}|$. Then we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item If $|\mathbf{k}|>|\mathbf{i}|+|\mathbf{j}|$, then $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}=0$. \item If $|\mathbf{k}|=|\mathbf{i}|+|\mathbf{j}|$ and $\mathbf{k}\neq \mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$, then $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}=0$. \item If $\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$, then $$c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}={i_1+j_1 \choose i_1}\cdot \ldots \cdot {i_e+j_e \choose i_e}.$$ \end{enumerate}
conclusions: If $|\mathbf{k}|>|\mathbf{i}|+|\mathbf{j}|$, then $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}=0$.
If $|\mathbf{k}|=|\mathbf{i}|+|\mathbf{j}|$ and $\mathbf{k}\neq \mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$, then $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}=0$.
If $\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}$, then $$c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}={i_1+j_1 \choose i_1}\cdot \ldots \cdot {i_e+j_e \choose i_e}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The structural constants vanish above total degree |i|+|j|, and in degree |i|+|j| they are the additive binomial coefficients.
nodes.label: newton

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.14
nodes.statement: It is clear for $\text{\textbf{i}}=\mathbf{0}$ or $\text{\textbf{j}}=\mathbf{0}$, so we assume that $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\neq \mathbf{0}$. By a truncated version of the formula \cite[(14.1.1)]{Hazew}, we have (in the notation of Remark \ref{gderint}) $$c(\mathbf{w}_m)=\mathbf{w}_m+\mathbf{v}_m+\mathbf{s}_m,$$ where $\mathbf{s}_m=(S_1,\ldots,S_e)$ for some $S_1,\ldots,S_e$ belonging to the ideal $(\mathbf{w}_m\cdot \mathbf{v}_m)$. Therefore for every $r\in R$ we have $$\sum_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}} D_{\mathbf{j}}D_{\mathbf{i}}(r)\mathbf{v}_m^{\mathbf{i}}\mathbf{w}_m^{\mathbf{j}}= \sum_{\mathbf{k}} D_{\mathbf{k}}(r)(\mathbf{w}_m+\mathbf{v}_m+\mathbf{s}_m)^{\mathbf{k}}.$$ We get the result by comparing the coefficients at $\mathbf{v}_m^{\mathbf{i}}\mathbf{w}_m^{\mathbf{j}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the comultiplication as w+v+s with s in (w·v) and compare coefficients of v^i w^j.

nodes.name: Disturbance from the additive iterativity
nodes.statement: Note that for every $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}\neq \mathbf{0}$ we have the following: $$D_{\mathbf{j}}\circ D_{\mathbf{i}}={i_1+j_1 \choose i_1}\cdot\ldots\cdot{i_e+j_e \choose i_e}D_{\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}} +\mathcal{O}(D_{\mathbf{n}})_{0<|\mathbf{n}|<|\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}|},$$ where $\mathcal{O}(D_{\mathbf{n}})_{0<|\mathbf{n}|<|\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}|}$ is a $k$-linear combination of $D_{\mathbf{n}}$ for $0<|\mathbf{n}|<|\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}|$. We consider the quantity $\mathcal{O}(\cdot)$ as a ``disturbance from the additive iterativity'', because for the additive iterativity condition this linear combination is always zero. Lemma 3.13 from \cite{HK1} regards the case of $e=1$.
nodes.statement_short: D_j∘D_i equals the additive binomial term plus a linear combination of lower-order D_n.

nodes.name: Constants equal absolute constants of D[1]
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf{R}=(R,\mathbb{D})$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$-ring, then the ring of constants of $\mathbf{R}$ coincides with the ring of absolute constants of $(R,\mathbb{D}[1])$.
conclusions: the ring of constants of $\mathbf{R}$ coincides with the ring of absolute constants of $(R,\mathbb{D}[1])$
nodes.label: absconst

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.16
nodes.statement: It follows from Lemma \ref{newton}, that for any $\mathbf{i}\neq \mathbf{0}$, $D_{\mathbf{i}}$ is a $k$-linear combination of the compositions of the derivations $D_{(1,0,\ldots,0)},\ldots,D_{(0,\ldots,0,1)}$ which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: By Lemma 3.14 each D_i is a linear combination of compositions of the first-order derivations.

nodes.name: Height-one case and restricted Lie algebras
nodes.statement: For $m=1$, any finite group scheme of the form considered in this paper (i.e. any finite group scheme of the \emph{Frobenius height one}) is equivalent to a \emph{restricted Lie algebra} in the sense of the theorem on page 139 of \cite{MuAbel}. Hence a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation ($m=1$) on $R$ is equivalent to an action on $R$ of $e$ derivations satisfying the commutator and the $p$-th composition rules given by the corresponding restricted Lie algebra $\mathrm{Lie}(\mathfrak{g})$ (see \cite{MuAbel}).
nodes.statement_short: For m=1, g-derivations are actions of e derivations obeying the restricted Lie algebra rules of Lie(g).
nodes.label: plie

nodes.name: Étale extensions preserve g-iterativity
nodes.statement: Assume that $R\to S$ is \'{e}tale and $\mathbb{D}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $R$. Then the unique extension of $\mathbb{D}$ to $S$ in Proposition \ref{etalehs} is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation.
conclusions: the unique extension of $\mathbb{D}$ to $S$ in Proposition \ref{etalehs} is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation
nodes.label: etalegext

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.18
nodes.statement: The proof of the moreover part of \cite[theorem 27.2]{mat} may be applied here, similarly as in the proof of Proposition \ref{etalehs}.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt the moreover part of Matsumura's Theorem 27.2 as in Proposition 3.3.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.18 for schemes
nodes.statement: As before, Proposition \ref{etalegext} easily generalizes to $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on $k$-schemes.
nodes.label: etalegextsch

nodes.name: Wronskian theorem for g-derivations
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}[1]$-field and $C$ be its field of constants. Then for any positive integer $l$ and any $x_1,\ldots,x_l\in K$, the elements $x_1,\ldots,x_l$ are linearly independent over $C$ if and only if the rank of the following ``Wronskian matrix" $$\big(D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_j)\big)_{\mathbf{i}\in [p]^e,j\leqslant l}$$ is strictly smaller than $l$.
assumptions: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}[1]$-field and $C$ be its field of constants.
for any positive integer $l$ and any $x_1,\ldots,x_l\in K$
conclusions: the elements $x_1,\ldots,x_l$ are linearly independent over $C$ if and only if the rank of the following ``Wronskian matrix" $$\big(D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_j)\big)_{\mathbf{i}\in [p]^e,j\leqslant l}$$ is strictly smaller than $l$
nodes.statement_short: Linear (in)dependence over the constants is detected by the rank of the Wronskian matrix (D_i(x_j)), i in [p]^e.
nodes.label: wronskian

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.20
nodes.statement: Assume that $x_l=c_1x_1+\ldots+c_{l-1}x_{l-1}$ for some $c_1,\ldots, c_{l-1}\in C$. By Lemma \ref{absconst}, each $D_{\mathbf{i}}$ is $C$-linear. Hence we obtain that the rank of our Wronskian matrix is smaller than $l$ as in the standard case (see \cite[Thm. II.1]{kol1}). \\ Let the rank of the matrix $\big(D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_j)\big)_{\mathbf{i}\in [p]^e,j\leqslant l}$ be equal to $r<l$. After reordering $x_1,\ldots,x_l$, we may assume that the matrix $\big(D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_j)\big)_{\mathbf{i}\in [p]^e,j\leqslant r}$ has rank $r$. Therefore there exist $\lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_{r+1}\in K$, not all equal to $0$, such that for each tuple $\mathbf{k}$ we have \begin{equation} \sum\limits_{s=1}^{r+1}\lambda_sD_{\mathbf{k}}(x_s)=0.\tag{$*$} \end{equation} \noindent Reordering and dividing by $c_{r+1}$ if need be, we may assume that $c_{r+1}=1$. By Remark \ref{gderint2}, there are $c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}\in C$ such that for all tuples $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}$ we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}\circ D_{\mathbf{i}}=\sum_{\mathbf{k}}c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}D_{\mathbf{k}}.$$ Hence for $\mathbf{1}:=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ and every tuple $\mathbf{i}$ we get (using $(*)$ with $\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{1}$ for the last equality) \begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl} 0 & = & \sum\limits_{s=1}^{r+1}D_{\mathbf{1}}(\lambda_s)D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_s)+\sum\limits_{s=1}^{r+1}\lambda_sD_{\mathbf{1}}(D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_s)) \\ & = & \sum\limits_{s=1}^{r}D_{\mathbf{1}}(\lambda_s)D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_s)+\sum\limits_{\mathbf{l}}c_{\mathbf{1},\mathbf{i}}^{\mathbf{l}}\sum\limits_{s=1}^{r+1}\lambda_sD_{\mathbf{l}}(x_s) \\ & = & \sum\limits_{s=1}^{r}D_{\mathbf{1}}(\lambda_s)D_{\mathbf{i}}(x_s). \end{IEEEeqnarray*} Thus $D_{(1,0,\ldots,0)}(\lambda_s)=0$ for every $s\leqslant r$. After similar reasoning for the derivations $D_{(0,1,0,\ldots,0)},\ldots,D_{(0,\ldots,0,1)}$ we get $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{r+1}\in C$. By setting $\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{0}$ in $(*)$, we obtain that $x_1,\ldots,x_l$ are linearly dependent over $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Constants make each D_i C-linear for one direction; for the other, differentiate a minimal dependence relation among Wronskian columns to show its coefficients are constants.

nodes.name: Wronskian dependence relation (*)
nodes.statement: \sum\limits_{s=1}^{r+1}\lambda_sD_{\mathbf{k}}(x_s)=0.\tag{$*$}

nodes.name: Degree of K over its constants
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}$-field and $C$ its field of constants. Then we have $$[K:C]\leqslant p^e.$$
assumptions: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}$-field and $C$ its field of constants.
conclusions: $$[K:C]\leqslant p^e.$$
nodes.label: dimconstants

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.21
nodes.statement: Let $l=p^e+1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_l\in K$. The rank of the corresponding Wronskian matrix from Proposition \ref{wronskian} is at most $p^e$, since there are only $p^e$ operators of the form $D_{\mathbf{i}}$. By Proposition \ref{wronskian}, $x_1,\ldots,x_l$ are linearly dependent over $C$.
nodes.statement_short: The Wronskian matrix has at most p^e rows, so any p^e+1 elements are dependent over C.

nodes.name: Degree of imperfection
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p$. Then $[K:K^p]=p^l$, where $l\in {\mathds{N}}\cup \{\infty\}$. We call $l$ the \emph{degree of imperfection} of $K$.

nodes.name: Linear disjointness of constants and étale extensions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ be an extension of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields. Let $C_K$ (resp. $C_L$) be the constant field of $\mathbf{K}$ (resp. $\mathbf{L}$). Then we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item The field $K$ is linearly disjoint from $C_L$ over $C_K$. \item If $\mathbf{K}$ is strict (see Def. \ref{firstdefstrict}(2)), then the extension $K\subseteq L$ is separable. \item If the extension $K\subseteq L$ is \'{e}tale and $K$ has a finite degree of imperfection, then $\mathbf{K}$ is strict if and only if $\mathbf{L}$ is strict. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The field $K$ is linearly disjoint from $C_L$ over $C_K$.
If $\mathbf{K}$ is strict (see Def. \ref{firstdefstrict}(2)), then the extension $K\subseteq L$ is separable.
If the extension $K\subseteq L$ is \'{e}tale and $K$ has a finite degree of imperfection, then $\mathbf{K}$ is strict if and only if $\mathbf{L}$ is strict.
nodes.statement_short: K is linearly disjoint from C_L over C_K; strict K gives separable extensions; strictness transfers along étale extensions of finite imperfection degree.
nodes.label: constantdisjoint

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.22
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we apply Lemma \ref{wronskian} as in the standard case (see \cite[Cor. 1, p. 87]{kol1}). \\ The item $(2)$ follows directly from $(1)$ using \cite[Thm. 26.4]{mat}. \\ The right-to-left implication in $(3)$ is clear (and only the condition $L^p\cap K=K^p$ is used). For the left-to-right implication, the \'{e}tale assumption implies that $[L:L^p]=[K:K^p]$ and $KL^p=L$. Since $L^p\subseteq C_L$, by $(1)$ (used for the second equality below) we get $$[L:L^p]=[K:K^p]=[KC_L:C_L]=[L:C_L].$$ Since $[L:L^p]$ is finite, we get $C_L=L^p$.
nodes.statement_short: Wronskian argument for (1), Matsumura 26.4 for (2), and a degree count [L:L^p]=[L:C_L] for (3).

nodes.name: F-derivation and G-derivation
nodes.statement: We define the following. \begin{enumerate} \item An \emph{$F$-derivation} on $V$ is a direct system of $F[m]$-derivations on $V$. \item A \emph{$G$-derivation} is a $\widehat{G}$-derivation (see Section \ref{gpschemetrun} for the definition of $\widehat{G}$). \item Similarly we get the notions of an $F$-derivation and a $G$-derivation on $R$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: An F-derivation is a direct system of F[m]-derivations; a G-derivation is a Ĝ-derivation.

nodes.name: F-iterativity and algebraic actions
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item As in Remarks \ref{gderint}, \ref{gderint2}, any $F$-derivation is an $e$-dimensional HS-derivation which satisfies the \emph{$F$-iterativity law}. \item Note that a $G$-derivation on $V$ (i.e. a direct system of group scheme actions of $G[m]$ on $V$) is \emph{not} the same as an algebraic action of $G$ on $V$. Clearly, any algebraic action of $G$ on $V$ gives a $G$-derivation by restricting the action of $G$ to $G[m]$ for each $m$. The difference between these two notions is easy to observe for $R=k[t]$ and $G=\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}$. If $\mathbb{D}$ is a $\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}$-derivation on $R$ (i.e. an iterative HS-derivation on $R$), then $\mathbb{D}$ comes from a $\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}$-action on $\mathrm{Spec}(R)$ if and only if there is $n$ such that for all $i>n$, we have $D_i(t)=0$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: F-derivations are HS-derivations obeying the F-iterativity law; G-derivations are weaker than algebraic G-actions.

nodes.name: Canonical F-derivation
nodes.statement: Let $R=k\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket$ and $K=k((\mathbf{X}))$. Similarly as in \cite[Section 3.2]{HK1}, we define a \emph{canonical $F$-derivation} on $R$ and $K$. As a $k$-algebra map, it is defined on $R$ as follows $$\mathbb{D}^F=\mathrm{ev}_F:R\to R\llbracket Y_1,\ldots,Y_e\rrbracket,\ \ \mathbb{D}^F(f)=f(F).$$ By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $\mathbb{D}^F$ uniquely extends to an $F$-derivation on $K$ which we also call canonical and also denote by $\mathbb{D}^F$. For any $m$, we call $\mathbb{D}^F[m]$ (on $R$ or on $K$) a \emph{canonical $F[m]$-derivation}.
nodes.statement_short: On k[[X]] the canonical F-derivation is evaluation f -> f(F), extended uniquely to k((X)).
nodes.label: canex

nodes.name: Non-isomorphic formal groups with equal truncations
nodes.statement: We point out here that for a given $\mathfrak{g}$, there may exist non-isomorphic formal groups $F_1,F_2$ such that $F_1[m]=\mathfrak{g}=F_2[m]$.

nodes.name: The canonical F-derivation is strict
nodes.statement: The canonical $F$-derivation (equivalently, $F[m]$-derivation) is strict.
conclusions: The canonical $F$-derivation (equivalently, $F[m]$-derivation) is strict.
nodes.label: canstrict

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.26
nodes.statement: We introduce the following notation: $$\partial^F_1=D_{(1,0,\ldots,0)},\ldots,\partial^F_e=D_{(0,\ldots,0,1)}.$$ Let $i\leqslant e$ and $f\in K$. By the chain rule, we get \begin{equation} \partial^F_i(f)=\Big(\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial Y_j}(\mathbf{X},0)\Big)_{i,j}\cdot \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_1},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_e}\Big).\tag{$*$} \end{equation} Let $J$ denote the Jacobian matrix appearing in $(*)$. Then $J$ is the matrix of the derivative (at $\mathbf{0}$) of the formal map which is the ``$F$-multiplication by $\mathbf{X}$''. Since this formal map is (formally) invertible, the matrix $J$ is non-singular. Therefore $f$ belongs to the field of constants if and only if $\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_i}=0$ for each $i$. The latter condition occurs if and only if $f$ is a $p$-th power, so the result is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Chain rule expresses the first-order operators via an invertible Jacobian times partial derivatives, so constants are p-th powers.

nodes.name: Chain rule for first-order operators (*)
nodes.statement: \partial^F_i(f)=\Big(\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial Y_j}(\mathbf{X},0)\Big)_{i,j}\cdot \Big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_1},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial X_e}\Big).\tag{$*$}

nodes.name: Canonical G-derivation on k(G)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{O}_G$ be the local ring of $G$ at the identity. Since $G$ is a smooth variety over $k$, $\mathcal{O}_G$ is a regular local ring. Let $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_e)$ be a sequence of local parameters in $\mathcal{O}_G$. By \cite[Thm 30.6(i)]{mat}, the ring $\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_G$ is the power series ring in the variables $\mathbf{x}$. If $F=\widehat{G}$, then $F(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{Y})\in \mathcal{O}_G\llbracket \mathbf{Y}\rrbracket$ (the group action is algebraic!). Hence $\mathcal{O}_G$ is a $G$-subring (after identifying $\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{X}$) of $(k\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket,\mathbb{D}^F)$. Therefore the field of rational functions $k(G)$ has a natural $G$-derivation on it which we call the \emph{canonical $G$-derivation} on $k(G)$. We also get a canonical $G[m]$-derivation on $k(G)$. \\ If $G$ is affine, then we also have a canonical $G$-derivation on $k[G]$. The natural extensions $$k[G]\subseteq K\llbracket \mathbf{X}\rrbracket,\ \ \ k(G)\subseteq K((\mathbf{X})),$$ where the local parameters on $G$ are understood as variables as in \cite[Thm 30.6(i)]{mat}, are $G$-extensions by our construction.
nodes.statement_short: Local parameters at the identity embed O_G into k[[X]] compatibly with F=Ĝ, giving canonical G-derivations on k(G) (and k[G]).
nodes.label: cangex

nodes.name: Quotient by a g-derivation
nodes.statement: We have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item The quotient scheme $V/\mathfrak{g}$ exists. \item If $V=\mathrm{Spec}(R)$, then $V/\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Spec}(C_{\mathbb{D}})$, where $C_{\mathbb{D}}$ is the ring of absolute constants of $\mathbf{R}$ (see Definition \ref{firstdefstrict}(3)). \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The quotient scheme $V/\mathfrak{g}$ exists.
$V/\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Spec}(C_{\mathbb{D}})$, where $C_{\mathbb{D}}$ is the ring of absolute constants of $\mathbf{R}$
nodes.label: quotient

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.28
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we quote \cite[Thm 1(A), p. 111]{MuAbel}. \\ By the proof of \cite[Thm 1(A), p. 111]{MuAbel} we have $V/\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{Spec}(C')$ where $$C'=\{r\in R\ |\ \mathbb{D}(r)=r\}.$$ Clearly $C'$ coincides with $C_{\mathbb{D}}$ giving $(2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Quote Mumford's quotient theorem; its proof identifies the quotient with the invariants, i.e. the absolute constants.

nodes.name: Freeness of the action and [K:C]=p^e
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{D}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}[1]$-derivation on a field $K$ with the field of constants $C$. Using Proposition \ref{wronskian}, it is easy to see that if $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in K$ are linearly independent over $C$, then $\mathbb{D}(x_1),\ldots,\mathbb{D}(x_n)\in K[\mathbf{v}_1]$ are linearly independent over $K$. Therefore the induced $K$-linear map $$\widetilde{\mathbb{D}}:K\otimes_CK\to K[\mathbf{v}_1],\ \ \ \ \ \ \widetilde{\mathbb{D}}(a_1\otimes b_1+\ldots+a_n\otimes b_n)=a_1\mathbb{D}(b_1)+\ldots+a_n\mathbb{D}(b_n)$$ is an embedding. Since we have $$\dim_KK\otimes_CK=[K:C]\leqslant p^e,\ \ \ \dim_KK[\mathbf{v}_1]=p^e,$$ the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $[K:C]=p^e$, \item the map $\widetilde{\mathbb{D}}$ is onto, \item the map $\widetilde{\mathbb{D}}$ is an isomorphism. \end{enumerate} \noindent In terms of group scheme actions, the above equivalences mean that the action of $\mathfrak{g}$ on $\mathrm{Spec}(K)$ is free if and only if $[K:C]=p^e$, and if this action is free, then the corresponding quotient $\mathrm{Spec}(C)=\mathrm{Spec}(K)/\mathfrak{g}$ is a good quotient. Note that the general theorem about group scheme actions \cite[Thm 1(B), p. 112]{MuAbel} gives the left-to-right implication above.
nodes.statement_short: The g-action on Spec(K) is free iff [K:C]=p^e, equivalently the induced map K⊗_C K -> K[v_1] is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: actioncom

nodes.name: Strictness via the Frobenius factorization
nodes.statement: Let $V^{\mathrm{Fr}^m}$ be $V$ twisted by the $m$-th power of the Frobenius automorphism as in Section \ref{gpschemetrun}. From the universal property of quotients, there is a unique morphism $\Psi$ making the following diagram commutative \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{4pc} \xymatrix{V \ar[d]_{\mathrm{Fr}^m_V} \ar[r]^{}& V/\mathfrak{g} \ar[dl]_{\Psi}\\ V^{\mathrm{Fr}^m} . } \end{equation*} If $V=\mathrm{Spec}(R)$ and $m=1$, then $\mathbf{R}$ is strict if and only if $\Psi$ is an isomorphism. It is also easy to see that for a reduced $R$ and arbitrary $m$, $\mathbf{R}$ is strict if and only if $\Psi$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: For reduced R, strictness means the induced map V/g -> V^{Fr^m} is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: factorstrict

nodes.name: The constants carry an induced action
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{D}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $R$ and $C$ be the ring of constants of $(R,\mathbb{D})$. Then we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item $C$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subring. \item A $\mathfrak{g}$-action on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$ naturally induces a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-action on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$, hence $C$ is naturally a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-ring. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $\mathbb{D}$ be a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $R$ and $C$ be the ring of constants of $(R,\mathbb{D})$.
conclusions: $C$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subring.
A $\mathfrak{g}$-action on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$ naturally induces a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-action on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$, hence $C$ is naturally a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-ring.
nodes.statement_short: The constants form a g-subring carrying a natural g[m-1]^{Fr}-structure.
nodes.label: deronc

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.31
nodes.statement: We work on the level of group scheme actions. By Theorem \ref{quotient}(2), we have $\mathrm{Spec}(C)=\mathrm{Spec}(R)/\mathfrak{g}[1]$. As in the case of the usual group actions (one can work it out on the level of rational points), we get the induced action of $\mathbb{D}$ on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$ (since $\mathfrak{g}[1]$ is normal in $\mathfrak{g}$) giving $(1)$. For $(2)$, a similar argument gives a natural action of $\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{g}[1]$ on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$. By Remark \ref{gm}, we have $$\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}\cong \mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{g}[1],$$ which proves $(2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Spec(C) is the quotient by the normal subgroup g[1], so g and g/g[1] ≅ g[m-1]^{Fr} act on it.

nodes.name: Explicit action on constants
nodes.statement: We can describe the $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-action on $\mathrm{Spec}(C)$ from Lemma \ref{deronc}(2) more specifically, since it is given by $(D_{p\mathbf{j}}|_C)_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}$. Hence for any $c\in C$ and $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, we get the following: $$D_{p\mathbf{j}}(D_{p\mathbf{i}}(c))=\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\left(c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}\right)^pD_{p\mathbf{k}}(c).$$
nodes.statement_short: The induced action on constants is given by the operators D_{pj}, with structural constants raised to the p-th power.
nodes.label: dpidpj

nodes.name: Ideals generated by selected operators are HS-ideals
nodes.statement: For $i\leqslant e$ and $j<m$, we define $(p^j)_i\in [p^m]^{\times e}$ as a sequence consisting of zeroes, except for the $i$-th coordinate where it has $p^j$. Assume $R$ is a $\mathfrak{g}$-ring and let $\mathcal{P}$ be a subset of $[p^m]^{\times e}$ such that $$\{(p^j)_i\ |\ i\leqslant e,j<m\}\subseteq \mathcal{P}.$$ Then for any $B\subset R$, the ideal generated by the set $$B_{\mathcal{P}}=\{D_{\mathbf{k}}(b)\ |\ b\in B,\mathbf{k}\in \mathcal{P}\}$$ is an HS-ideal.
assumptions: let $\mathcal{P}$ be a subset of $[p^m]^{\times e}$ such that $$\{(p^j)_i\ |\ i\leqslant e,j<m\}\subseteq \mathcal{P}.$$
conclusions: for any $B\subset R$, the ideal generated by the set $$B_{\mathcal{P}}=\{D_{\mathbf{k}}(b)\ |\ b\in B,\mathbf{k}\in \mathcal{P}\}$$ is an HS-ideal
nodes.statement_short: To generate an HS-ideal it suffices to close under the operators D_k with k in a set containing the p-power coordinate indices.
nodes.label: hsideal

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.33
nodes.statement: It follows from Remark \ref{gderint2} and Lemma \ref{newton}.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from the structural-constant description of g-iterativity and Lemma 3.14.

nodes.name: Existence of strict g-field extensions
nodes.statement: Any $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{K}$ has a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension.
conclusions: has a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field extension
nodes.label: gstrictexist

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.34
nodes.statement: We consider the theory of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields as a universal theory in the language of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields (containing $-$ and $\div$). Then any $\mathfrak{g}$-field embeds into an existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-field. Therefore, it is enough to prove that existentially closed $\mathfrak{g}$-fields are strict, so we may assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is existentially closed. Assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is not strict, i.e. there is $a\in K\setminus K^p$ which is a constant of $\mathbf{K}$. To reach a contradiction (with the assumption that $\mathbf{K}$ is existentially closed), it is enough to find a $\mathfrak{g}$-extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ such that $a^{1/p}\in L$. Let $C$ denote the field of constants of $\mathbf{K}$ and $B$ be a $p$-basis of $C$ over $K^p$ such that $a\in B$. \\ \\ {\bf Claim 1} \\ There is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ extending the one we have on $K$ and such that for each $b\in B$ and each $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}(b^{1/p})=(D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b))^{1/p}.$$ \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim 1] By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2) and Remark \ref{dpidpj}, $$\mathbb{D}':=\left(D_{p\mathbf{j}}|_C\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}$$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-derivation on $C$. Let $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}:C\cong C^{1/p}$, and $\mathbb{D}''$ be $\mathbb{D}'$ transported to $C^{1/p}$ using $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}$. Then $\mathbb{D}''$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ and by the construction it has the required properties (see also Lemma \ref{transport} and the proof of Proposition \ref{strictext}). \end{proof} We consider the following rings (the set $B$ indexes the variables): $$R:=K\left[X_b^{(\mathbf{i})}\ |\ \mathbf{i}\in [p^m]^{\times e},\ b\in B\right],$$ $$R':=K\left[X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\ |\ \mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e},\ b\in B\right];$$ where for each $b\in B$, $X_b$ is identified with $X_b^{(0,\ldots,0)}$. We put a $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R$ which is $\mathfrak{g}$-extending $\mathbf{K}$ in the following way: $$D_{\mathbf{j}}\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{i})}\right):=\sum_{\mathbf{f}\in [p^m]^{\times e}}c^{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}X_b^{(\mathbf{f})}.$$ Then $R'$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-subring of $R$. Let us define a subset $W\subset R'$ as follows: $$W:=\left\{\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)\ |\ \mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e},\ b\in B\right\}.$$ We define the following $K$-algebra map $$\Psi:R'\to C^{1/p},\ \ \Psi\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)=D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)^{1/p}$$ and let $\mathfrak{m}=\ker(\Psi)$. By Claim 1, $\Psi$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-map, so $\mathfrak{m}$ is a maximal $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-ideal of $R'$ containing $W$. We will show that the $\mathfrak{g}$-ideal $J$ in $R$ which is $\mathfrak{g}$-generated by $\mathfrak{m}$ is prime (then we can take $L$ as the field of fractions of $R/J$). Let us order the set $[p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ as $\mathbf{k}_{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{k}_{(p^{(m-1)e})}$ such that for $i\leqslant j$, we have $|\mathbf{k}_{(i)}|\leqslant |\mathbf{k}_{(j)}|$ (in particular $\mathbf{k}_{(1)}=(0,\ldots,0)$). We also order $B=(b_s)_{s<\kappa}$ such that $b_0=a$. \\ \\ {\bf Claim 2} \\ There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types: $$\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum _{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{t,i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})};$$ where $b\in B$, $s<\kappa$, $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, $j\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}$ and $\alpha_{i,l},\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}\in K$. \begin{proof}[Proof of Claim 2] We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps. In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators. In Step (0,2), we consider two cases. \\ Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators. \\ Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators. In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$. Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$. \end{proof} By Lemma \ref{hsideal}, it is enough to apply to the generators from Claim 2 the operators $D_{\mathbf{i}}$, where $\mathbf{i}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ or where $\mathbf{i}$ is of the form $(p^{m-1})_i$ (see Lemma \ref{hsideal} for the definition of $(p^{m-1})_i$). If $\mathbf{i}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ then we get elements of $\mathfrak{m}$, so we may focus on the other case. To treat the first type of the generators from Claim 2, we just need to use that there is $\mathbf{l}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$ such that $\mathbf{i}=p\mathbf{l}$. We obtain the following: \begin{IEEEeqnarray*}{rCl} D_{p\mathbf{l}}\left(\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)\right) & = & \left(D_{\mathbf{l}}\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{l}}\left(D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b)\right) \\ & = & \left(\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}} c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}X_b^{(\mathbf{k})}\right)^p - \sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}} (c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}})^pD_{p\mathbf{k}}(b) \\ & = & \sum_{\mathbf{k}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}} \left(c_{\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}}^{\mathbf{k}}\right)^p\left(\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{k})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}}(b)\right), \end{IEEEeqnarray*} where the second equality holds by Remark \ref{dpidpj}, since $b\in C$. Hence we get that $D_{p\mathbf{l}}((X_b^{(\mathbf{j})})^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b))$ belongs to the ideal generated by $W$ in $R'$, so it also belongs to $\mathfrak{m}$. After applying $D_{\mathbf{i}}$ to the second type of generators, by Lemma \ref{newton} we get the following: $$D_{\mathbf{i}}\left( X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})} \right) = $$ $$ {\mathbf{k}_{(j)}+\mathbf{i}\choose \mathbf{i}}X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)}+\mathbf{i})} + \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}d_{i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)}+\mathbf{i})}\right)^l + Q,$$ for some $d_{i,l}\in K$, where $${\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}\choose \mathbf{i}}:={i_1+j_1 \choose i_1}\cdot \ldots \cdot {i_e+j_e \choose i_e},$$ and where $$Q\in K\left[X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{r})},\ X^{(\mathbf{j})}_{b_s}\ |\ t<s,\ \mathbf{r}\in [p^m]^{\times e},\ \mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}\right].$$ We forget now about the HS-differential structure on $R$ and $J$. The obtained set of generators of $J$ is of the form $J_1\cup J_2$, where $J_1\subseteq \mathfrak{m}$ and $J_2\subseteq R'[X_{\gamma}]_{\gamma\in \mathcal{I}}$ (after renaming variables), and $$\mathcal{I}:=\kappa\times \{1,\ldots,e\}\times (\mathbf{k}_{i})_{i\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}}$$ with the lexicographical order. Moreover, there is a subset $\mathcal{I}_0\subset \mathcal{I}$ such that without loss of generality (since $p$ does not divide ${\mathbf{k}_{(j)}+\mathbf{i}\choose \mathbf{i}}$), we have $$J_2=\{X_{\gamma}-Q_{\gamma}\ |\ \gamma\in \mathcal{I}_0\},$$ where for each $\gamma\in \mathcal{I}_0$, $Q_{\gamma}\in R'[X_{\delta}]_{\delta<\gamma}$. Therefore, the ring $R/J$ is isomorphic to a polynomial ring over $R'/\mathfrak{m}$, so the ideal $J$ is prime.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to existentially closed K and adjoin p-th roots of a constant non-p-th power: build a g-ring R over K and show the g-ideal generated by a maximal g[m-1]-ideal is prime. Key step: Claim 2's triangular generators make R/J a polynomial ring.

nodes.name: Claim 1 (g[m-1]-derivation on C^{1/p})
nodes.statement: There is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ extending the one we have on $K$ and such that for each $b\in B$ and each $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, we have $$D_{\mathbf{j}}(b^{1/p})=(D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b))^{1/p}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The g[m-1]-derivation extends to C^{1/p} with D_j(b^{1/p}) = D_{pj}(b)^{1/p}.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 1
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{deronc}(2) and Remark \ref{dpidpj}, $$\mathbb{D}':=\left(D_{p\mathbf{j}}|_C\right)_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}$$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]^{\mathrm{Fr}}$-derivation on $C$. Let $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}:C\cong C^{1/p}$, and $\mathbb{D}''$ be $\mathbb{D}'$ transported to $C^{1/p}$ using $\mathrm{Fr}_C^{-1}$. Then $\mathbb{D}''$ is a $\mathfrak{g}[m-1]$-derivation on $C^{1/p}$ and by the construction it has the required properties (see also Lemma \ref{transport} and the proof of Proposition \ref{strictext}).
nodes.statement_short: Transport the g[m-1]^{Fr}-derivation (D_{pj}) on C to C^{1/p} via the inverse Frobenius.

nodes.name: Claim 2 (triangular generators of m)
nodes.statement: There is a set of generators of $\mathfrak{m}$ consisting of elements of the following two types: $$\left(X_b^{(\mathbf{j})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{j}}(b),\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(j)})} - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\sum _{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_{t,i,l}\left(X_{b_s}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(i)})}\right)^l - \sum_{t<s}\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}}\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}X_{b_t}^{(\mathbf{j})};$$ where $b\in B$, $s<\kappa$, $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, $j\in \{1,\ldots,p^{(m-1)e}\}$ and $\alpha_{i,l},\beta_{t,\mathbf{j}}\in K$.
nodes.statement_short: The maximal ideal m has generators that are either p-th power relations or triangular linear relations in the variables.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: We construct a required set of generators in $p^{(m-1)e}\cdot \kappa$ steps. In Step (0,1), we add $X^p-b_0$ to the (so far empty) set of generators. In Step (0,2), we consider two cases. \\ Case 1: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\notin K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case, we add the element $$\left(X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}\right)^p-D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)$$ to the set of generators. \\ Case 2: $D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)\in K^p(b_0)$. \\ In this case $$D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0)=\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pb_0^l,$$ for some $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{p-1}\in K$, and we add the element $$X_{b_0}^{(\mathbf{k}_{(2)})}-\sum_{l=0}^{p-1}\alpha_l^pX_{b_0}^l$$ to the set of generators. In Step (0,3), we proceed as in Step (0,2) with the field $K^p(b_0,D_{p\mathbf{k}_{(2)}}(b_0))$ replacing the field $K^p(b_0)$. Continuing like this, after $p^{(m-1)e}$ steps we obtain our desired set of generators for $b_0$. We continue in a similar way (although e.g. Step (1,1) already consist of two cases) for $(b_i)_{i>0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Transfinite step-by-step construction of generators, splitting at each step on whether the next value lies in the field generated so far.

nodes.name: Idea of the proof of Proposition 3.34; differential perfectness
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The proof above may seem to be technical, but the idea is very simple. For $\mathbf{j}\in [p^{m-1}]^{\times e}$, the value $D_{\mathbf{j}}(a^{1/p})$ is determined by Claim 1. For $i\leqslant e$, we set $D_{(p^{m-1})_i}(a^{1/p})$ as a new formal variable. The values of the remaining operators on $a^{1/p}$ are determined by the $\mathfrak{g}$-iterativity rule. \item \item The above proof may be also used to show that a $\mathfrak{g}$-field is strict if and only if it is \emph{differentially perfect}, i.e. each of its differential extension is separable. This generalizes a result of Kolchin (see Chapter II, Section 3., Proposition 5.(a) in \cite{kol1}). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The proof sets the top-order operators on a^{1/p} as new variables; it also shows strict iff differentially perfect.
nodes.label: values

nodes.name: Tensor product of g-rings
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-rings. Then there is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R\otimes_kS$ such that the natural maps $\mathbf{R}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-homomorphisms.
conclusions: there is a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-ring structure on $R\otimes_kS$ such that the natural maps $\mathbf{R}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$, $\mathbf{S}\to \mathbf{R}\otimes_k\mathbf{S}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-homomorphisms
nodes.label: forap

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.36
nodes.statement: It is convenient to show a more general result. Assume that $V,W$ are schemes over $k$ and $\mathbb{D}_V$ and $\mathbb{D}_W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-derivations on $V$ and $W$ respectively. As in the case of the usual group actions, we get a unique $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $V\times W$ such that the projections $V\times W\to V,W$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-invariant. By considering the affine schemes and dualizing, we get what we need.
nodes.statement_short: Product of g-schemes carries a unique diagonal action; dualize for affine schemes.

nodes.name: Amalgamation over strict g-fields
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}_1,\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}_2$ be $\mathfrak{g}$-field extensions and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is strict. Then $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ can be $\mathfrak{g}$-amalgamated over $\mathbf{K}$ into a $\mathfrak{g}$-field.
conclusions: $\mathbf{L}_1$ and $\mathbf{L}_2$ can be $\mathfrak{g}$-amalgamated over $\mathbf{K}$ into a $\mathfrak{g}$-field
nodes.label: lambdaap

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.37
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, we can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are separably closed (since separable algebraic extensions are \'{e}tale). Then $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is a subfield of $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Remark \ref{defgen}(5), it is a $\mathfrak{g}$-subfield. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint} (using Corollary \ref{dimconstants}), the $\mathfrak{g}$-field structure on $K^{\mathrm{sep}}$ is strict. Therefore we can assume that $K$ is separably closed as well. \\ The proof will be finished exactly as in \cite[Prop. 2.6]{Zieg2}. We can assume that $L_1,L_2$ are subfields of a big field $\Omega$ and that they are algebraically disjoint over $K$. By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}, the extension $K\subseteq L_1$ is separable. Since $K$ is separably closed, this extension is regular (see \cite[p. 367]{lang2002algebra}). By \cite[Thm. VIII 4.12]{lang2002algebra}, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$, thus $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ is a domain. By Lemma \ref{forap}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on $L_1\otimes_KL_2$ extending those on $L_1$ and $L_2$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext} again, we get the required $\mathfrak{g}$-structure on the field of fractions of $L_1\otimes_KL_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to separably closed fields via étale extension, then use regularity to make L1⊗_K L2 a domain with the tensor g-structure.

nodes.name: g is the truncation of a formal group law
nodes.statement: In this subsection, we assume that $\mathfrak{g}$ is of the form $W[m]$ for a formal group law $W$ (see Remark \ref{intgs}).

nodes.name: p-th root function lambda
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p$ and $\lambda$ be the following \emph{$p$-th root function}: $$\lambda:K\to K,\ \ \ \lambda(x)= \begin{cases} x^{1/p}\text{ for }x\in K^p, \\ 0\ \ \ \ \text{ for }x\notin K^p. \end{cases}$$
nodes.statement_short: λ(x) is the p-th root of x when x is a p-th power, and 0 otherwise.

nodes.name: Language L^lambda
nodes.statement: Let $L^{\lambda}$ be the language of rings expanded by a unary function symbol $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Language L_{e,m}
nodes.statement: Let $L_{e,m}$ be the language of $k$-algebras (so there are constants in the language for the elements of $k$) with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations.

nodes.name: Language L^lambda_{e,m}
nodes.statement: Let $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}=L^{\lambda}\cup L_{e,m}$.

nodes.name: L^lambda-extensions
nodes.statement: Each field of characteristic $p$ has a natural $L^{\lambda}$-structure and we have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item A field extension $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension if and only if $L^p\cap K=K^p$. \item If $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L_{e,m}$-extension and $\mathbf{K}$ is strict, then $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-extension. \item Suppose $R$ is a subring of a field $L$, $K$ is the field of fractions of $R$ and $R\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. Then $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Each field of characteristic $p$ has a natural $L^{\lambda}$-structure
conclusions: A field extension $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension if and only if $L^p\cap K=K^p$.
If $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L_{e,m}$-extension and $\mathbf{K}$ is strict, then $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-extension.
Then $K\subseteq L$ is an $L^{\lambda}$-extension.
nodes.statement_short: Characterization of L^λ-extensions and their behaviour under strictness and fraction fields.
nodes.label: lamb

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: The item $(1)$ is clear and $(2)$ follows from Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(2). The last item follows by an easy computation.
nodes.statement_short: (1) is clear, (2) follows from Lemma 3.22(2), (3) by computation.

nodes.name: Elementary extensions of separably closed g-fields
nodes.statement: Let us assume that $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-fields such that $K$ and $L$ are separably closed and that $K$ has finite imperfectness degree. Then the following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The fields $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. \item The $K$-algebra $L$ is \'{e}tale. \item The extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary (in the language of rings). \item The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary. \item The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L_{e,m}$-elementary. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ are $\mathfrak{g}$-fields such that $K$ and $L$ are separably closed and that $K$ has finite imperfectness degree
conclusions: The fields $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis.
The $K$-algebra $L$ is \'{e}tale.
The extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary (in the language of rings).
The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary.
The extension $\mathbf{K}\subseteq \mathbf{L}$ is $L_{e,m}$-elementary.
nodes.statement_short: For separably closed g-fields of finite imperfection degree: same p-basis ⇔ étale ⇔ elementary (in rings, L^λ_{e,m}, L_{e,m}).
nodes.label: elementaryetale

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: By the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.1]{Del1} and by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1}, the extension $K\subseteq L$ is elementary if and only if $K$ and $L$ have the same (absolute) $p$-basis. By \cite[Theorem 26.7]{mat}, it happens if and only if this extension is \'{e}tale, so we get the equivalence of $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$. \\ Since both the $\lambda$-function and the $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation are defined (over the field of the $p^m$-th powers) using the field operations and the elements of a $p$-basis, we get the equivalence of $(3)$ with $(4)$ and $(5)$.
nodes.statement_short: Delon's p-basis criterion for elementarity plus Matsumura 26.7; operators are definable from a p-basis.

nodes.name: Theory g-DF
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ be the theory of $\mathfrak{g}$-fields in the language $L_{e,m}$.

nodes.name: Theory g-DF_lambda
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}_{\lambda}$ be the theory of strict $\mathfrak{g}$-fields in the language $L_{e,m}^{\lambda}$ i.e. $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}_{\lambda}$ contains the natural interpretation of $\lambda$ and the following extra axiom: $$ orall x \Big((x
eq 0\ \wedge \ \lambda(x)=0)\ ightarrow\ (D_{(1,0,\ldots,0)}(x)
eq 0\ \vee\ \ldots \vee D_{(0,\ldots,0,1)}(x)
eq 0)\Big).$$
nodes.statement_short: Theory of strict g-fields in L^λ_{e,m}, with an axiom that non-p-th powers are non-constants.

nodes.name: Theory g-DCF
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ be the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ with the extra axioms for strict $\mathfrak{g}$-fields, and for separably closed fields of imperfectness degree $e$.

nodes.name: Theory g-DCF_lambda
nodes.statement: Similarly for $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$.

nodes.name: Consistency of g-DCF
nodes.statement: The theories $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ and $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ are consistent.
conclusions: The theories $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ and $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ are consistent.
nodes.label: consistent

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: We take the canonical $F$-derivation $\mathbb{D}^F$ on the field $K$ from Example \ref{canex}. By Proposition \ref{canstrict}, $\mathbf{K}$ is strict and clearly the imperfection degree of $K$ is $e$. By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, $\mathbb{D}^F$ extends to the separable closure of $K$ (a separable algebraic extension is \'{e}tale, see \cite[Thm. 26.7]{mat}). By Lemma \ref{constantdisjoint}(3), this extension is still strict. Since it is \'{e}tale, the degree of imperfection does not change.
nodes.statement_short: The canonical F-derivation on k((X)), extended to its separable closure, is a strict model of imperfection degree e.

nodes.name: Embedding over a common substructure
nodes.statement: Let us take $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{F}$ being a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. Then there is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-embedding of $\mathbf{F}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$.
assumptions: Let us take $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{F}$ being a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field and assume that $\mathbf{K}$ is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$.
conclusions: there is an $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-embedding of $\mathbf{F}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$
nodes.statement_short: A strict g-field embeds over a common L^λ_{e,m}-substructure into an elementary extension of a model of g-DCF_λ.
nodes.label: elemamal

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{defgen}(1), Proposition \ref{etalegext} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(3), we can assume that $K$ is a field. By Lemma \ref{lamb}(1), we have $K^p=L^p\cap K$. Since $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{L}$ is strict and hence $\mathbf{K}$ is strict as well. By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and Lemma \ref{lamb}(2), we can $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-amalgamate $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$ over $\mathbf{K}$ into a strict $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable, by \cite[Claim 2.2]{Del1} there is an elementary extension in the language of fields $L\preccurlyeq L'$ and a field embedding $\Upsilon:F'\to L'$ over $L$. The situation is described in the following diagram: \begin{equation*} \xymatrixcolsep{4pc} \xymatrix{ & & L'\\ & \mathbf{F}'\ar[ru]^{\Upsilon} & \\ \mathbf{F}\ar[ru]^{} & & \mathbf{L}\ar[lu]^{} \ar[uu]^{\preccurlyeq}\\ & \mathbf{K}\ar[ru]^{}\ar[lu]^{}. & } \end{equation*} By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale. The $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}'$ is strict, so by Corollary \ref{dimconstants}, we have $[F':(F')^p]\leqslant p^e$. Since the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is separable and $[L:L^p]=p^e$, by the equivalence between $(1)$ and $(2)$ in Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $L\subseteq F'$ is \'{e}tale. Then the extension $F'\subseteq L'$ is \'{e}tale as well. By Proposition \ref{etalegext}, there is a $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation on $L'$ extending the one on $F'$ (hence also extending the one on $L$). By Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, the extension $\mathbf{L}\subseteq \mathbf{L}'$ is $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-elementary and we are done.
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamate F and L into strict F', embed F' into an elementary field extension L' of L, and extend the g-derivation along étale maps.

nodes.name: Model companion for g-fields
nodes.statement: We have the following. \begin{enumerate} \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ has quantifier elimination in the language $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$. \item Each model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ embeds into a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$. \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$. \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is a model completion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}_{\lambda}$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ has quantifier elimination in the language $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$.
Each model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ embeds into a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$.
The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$.
The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is a model completion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}_{\lambda}$.
nodes.statement_short: g-DCF_λ has QE and is the model completion of g-DF_λ; g-DCF is the model companion of g-DF.
nodes.label: qegdcf

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: For $(1)$, we use the criterion from \cite[Theorem 13.1]{sacks} (and Proposition \ref{elemamal}) exactly as in \cite[3.1]{Zieg2}. \\ For $(2)$, let us take any $\mathfrak{g}$-field $\mathbf{F}$. By Proposition \ref{gstrictexist}, we may assume that $\mathbf{F}$ is strict. By Lemma \ref{consistent}, there is $\mathbf{L}\models \mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$. Clearly, $k$ with the trivial $\mathfrak{g}$-structure is a common $L^{\lambda}_{e,m}$-substructure of both $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{L}$. By Proposition \ref{elemamal}, $\mathbf{F}$ embeds into an elementary extension of $\mathbf{L}$, which is clearly a model of $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ as well. \\ By $(1)$, $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}_{\lambda}$ is model complete, so using Lemma \ref{lamb}(2) and Lemma \ref{elementaryetale}, we get that $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is model complete as well. By $(2)$, $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is a model companion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$, so we get $(3)$. \\ By Proposition \ref{lambdaap} and the item $(1)$, we get $(4)$.
nodes.statement_short: QE via Sacks' criterion and Proposition 4.4; embedding via strict extensions and consistency; model completeness transferred via Lemma 4.2.

nodes.name: Comments on g-DCF
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$ does not have the amalgamation property. The theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ does not have quantifier elimination and the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DCF}$ is not a model completion of the theory $\mathfrak{g}-\mathrm{DF}$. \item We have (after taking $k={\mathds{F}}_p$) $$\mathbb{G}_{\rm{a}}^e[m]-\mathrm{DCF} =\mathrm{SCH}_{p,e,m},$$ where $\mathrm{SCH}_{p,e,m}$ is the theory considered in \cite{K3}. \item If we take the algebraic group $U$ from Example \ref{gitex}(2), then a $U(1)$-field is the same as a field with two derivations $\partial_1,\partial_2$ such that $\partial_1^{(p)}=\partial_2$ and $\partial_2^{(p)}=0$. Hence $U(1)-\mathrm{DCF}$ corresponds to Wood's theory $2-\mathrm{DCF}$, see \cite{Wo2}. It should be possible to find algebraic groups governing the iterative rules for Wood's theories $m-\mathrm{DCF}$ for an arbitrary $m$. \item After dropping the iterativity assumptions rather strange things happen. In the case of characteristic zero, model companions exist and are analyzed in \cite{MS2}. In the case of positive characteristic, it is shown in \cite[Prop 7.2]{MS2} that (in our terminology) the theory of fields with $m$-truncated $e$-dimensional HS-derivations has a model companion if and only if $m=1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: g-DF lacks amalgamation; G_a^e[m]-DCF equals SCH_{p,e,m}; relation to Wood's 2-DCF; non-iterative case has a model companion only for m=1.

nodes.name: Language L_e
nodes.statement: Let $L_e$ be the language of $k$-algebras with $e$-dimensional HS-derivations.

nodes.name: Theory F-DF
nodes.statement: Let $F-\mathrm{DF}$ be the theory of $F$-fields.

nodes.name: Theory F-DCF
nodes.statement: Let $F-\mathrm{DCF}$ be the theory $F-\mathrm{DF}$ with the extra axioms for strict $F$-fields, and for separably closed fields of imperfection degree $e$.

nodes.name: Transport of g-derivations
nodes.statement: Let $f\in \mathrm{Aut}(k)$ and let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an isomorphism of rings extending $f$. For any $\mathfrak{g}$-derivation $\mathbb{D}$ on $R$, we define: $$\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}:S\to S[\mathbf{v}_m],\ \ \ \mathbb{D}^{\varphi}:=\varphi[\mathbf{v}_m]\circ \mathbb{D}\circ \varphi^{-1}.$$ Then $\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$-derivation, where $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$ is the group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ twisted by $f$.
assumptions: Let $f\in \mathrm{Aut}(k)$ and let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an isomorphism of rings extending $f$.
conclusions: Then $\mathbb{D}^{\varphi}$ is a $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$-derivation, where $\mathfrak{g}^{f}$ is the group scheme $\mathfrak{g}$ twisted by $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugating a g-derivation by a ring isomorphism over f gives a g^f-derivation.
nodes.label: transport

nodes.name: Smallest strict F-field extension
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}=(K,\mathbb{D})$ be an $F$-field. Then there is a smallest strict $F$-field extending $\mathbf{K}$.
conclusions: there is a smallest strict $F$-field extending $\mathbf{K}$
nodes.label: strictext
